fatal_errors: The proposed material is native-oxide Q235 carbon steel, whereas the target system is an atmospheric-plasma-sprayed AlCoCrFeNi coating on SS316L followed by annealing.
The governing target intervention—approximately 150 µm HEA coating and 2 h annealing, particularly at 550 °C—is entirely absent.
The proposed 3.5 wt% NaCl exposure near 70 °C does not reconstruct either the target 3.5 wt% H2SO4 electrochemical test or the 900 °C cyclic Na2SO4/NaCl/V2O5 hot-corrosion tests.

The cited evidence concerns cracking in an Al-HEA coating and explicitly attributes it to internal coating stresses without corrosion products in the cracks; it does not support thermal-mismatch cracking of native oxide on Q235.
Temperature, thermal cycling, oxygen transport, solution kinetics, and oxide cracking are changed together, so the experiment does not isolate thermal-stress-induced cracking as the governing cause.
explanation: The response addresses corrosion onset and proposes measurable electrochemical and microscopy outcomes, but it does not reconstruct the hidden study. The target hypothesis centers on APS AlCoCrFeNi-coated SS316L, microstructural optimization by 550 °C annealing, grain refinement and BCC/FCC phase balance, and formation of Al- and Cr-rich protective oxides. The generated hypothesis instead invokes native-oxide cracking on Q235 during mild chloride exposure. Its predictions of higher corrosion current, lower polarization resistance, and more pits are testable, but they neither match the target intervention nor its reported comparison in which coating and annealing improve resistance. The experiment also lacks isothermal elevated-temperature and mechanically precracked controls needed to distinguish thermal cycling from ordinary temperature-accelerated electrochemistry. Most importantly, E1 is materially non-transferable and partly conflicts with the claimed corrosion mechanism, making the central causal assertion unsupported.
